title: Every named US hurricane was a woman.
description:
Every named US hurricane was a woman. From 1953, when the US dropped a phonetic-alphabet naming scheme for storms, until 1979, hurricanes and tropical storms got female names only. No exceptions.

Storms got described the way lazy jokes describe women. Forecasters called them 'temperamental', said they were 'flirting' with the coast. It was treated as charming. Female meteorologists were not charmed.

Florida feminist who founded the United States' first rape treatment centre and led the campaign to end female-only hurricane names, arguing that women 'deeply resent being arbitrarily associated with disaster'.

Men's names arrived in 1978, then 1979. The Eastern Pacific added male names first; the Atlantic and Gulf followed the next year. Some forecasters warned male-named storms would not be taken seriously.

A later study found the opposite: people underestimate female-named hurricanes, and it has cost lives.

Sources:
- https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/aboutnames_history.shtml - National Hurricane Center (NOAA), official naming-history page, read in full. Established that West Indies hurricanes were long named after the saint's day they struck, that Australian meteorologist Clement Wragge began giving storms women's names before the end of the 19th century, that the 1941 novel 'Storm' by George R. Stewart popularised a woman's name for a storm and the habit spread among US Army and Navy meteorologists in the Second World War, that in 1953 the United States dropped a two-year-old phonetic-alphabet naming scheme and began using women's names exclusively, that the practice of naming hurricanes only after women ended in 1978 when the Eastern North Pacific lists added men's names, followed by the Atlantic and Gulf lists in 1979, and that the World Meteorological Organization now runs rotating name lists, retiring a name only when a storm carrying it was especially deadly or costly.
- https://www.history.com/articles/why-hurricanes-and-tropical-storms-were-only-named-after-women - HISTORY (Becky Little, 1 August 2017, updated 27 May 2025), read in full. Established that from roughly 1953 to 1979 US hurricanes and tropical storms were named only after women, that forecasters described storms in sexist terms such as 'temperamental' or 'flirting' with the coast, that Roxcy Bolton, a Florida feminist credited with founding the United States' first rape treatment centre, was a leading campaigner who helped persuade forecasters to end female-only naming, arguing per her New York Times obituary that women 'deeply resent being arbitrarily associated with disaster', that campaigns by Bolton and others led to men's names returning from 1979, that some critics at the time argued male-named storms would not be taken seriously, and that a 2016 study (cited by History.com, not independently read here) found the opposite: female-named hurricanes are perceived as less dangerous and have historically caused more deaths as a result.
